tracks.intro: A careless road killer turns into a snack-loving child, a stern teacher and a gambler who keeps guaranteeing the next win. Listen for ambition made literal and words chaining together by sound.

notes.title: A road idiom made gruesomely literal
notes.body: 马路杀手 is a familiar insult for a dangerously bad driver: literally a “road killer.” Here the next line supplies an actual victim, turning an everyday exaggeration into cartoon gore. That also wrong-foots the English title: this “Hitman” starts as someone who was not even paying attention, not a cool professional assassin.

notes.title: A deliberately inadequate apology
notes.body: After grinding someone to a pulp, the speaker worries about whether the victim will hold a grudge. The mismatch makes the joke: 记仇 belongs to the manageable world of social slights, and “hope he doesn’t” sounds almost considerate. Repeating the little worry lets politeness outlive the person it is supposedly concerned for.

notes.title: Flying high, drinking 高乐高
notes.body: 高乐高 is ColaCao, a cocoa-drink brand. Its Chinese name begins and ends with 高 gāo, “high.” The previous wish to “fly higher” moves from ambition to a literal airplane, then lands in this little chain of repeated sounds. A grand promise for the new year becomes an ordinary in-flight snack, preparing the snack-loving child who emerges next.

notes.title: Temple Run in the middle of the flight
notes.body: 神庙逃亡 is Temple Run. In his own 2025 recommendations for Perfectly Imperfect, Jackzebra said he plays it on planes, trains and before shows. The airplane routine here therefore meets a specific habit he has described. Inside the verse, the familiar phone game also helps make the grotesque road killer suddenly look like the snack-loving little boy he announces next.

sources.label: Jackzebra’s own recommendations for Perfectly Imperfect (2025)

notes.title: A branded gift pack
notes.body: 旺旺大礼包 is a Want Want assortment of packaged snacks. 大礼包 makes it a whole gift bundle rather than one treat, and 捧着 pictures someone cradling it in both hands. After the “little boy in my heart,” the pose supplies the childhood feeling through a specific, graspable object. It is snack abundance rather than a luxury-brand flex.

notes.title: Reveal

phrase.en: You won't know until I say it

notes.body: This is the first half of a conversational reveal formula: you would never know until someone said it, and hearing it gives you a shock. Its paired negatives and rhyming endings build a tiny suspense routine. Instead of delivering a grand revelation, the verse pivots into telling the listener they are too slow to keep up.

notes.title: Eliminated

phrase.en: times are going to leave you behind

notes.body: 淘汰 is elimination: an obsolete product, an unsuccessful contestant, or someone unable to keep pace gets removed. “Left behind” is gentler than that threat. After promising never to grow old, the speaker treats the listener’s slowness as grounds for expulsion from the present, borrowing the stern vocabulary of competitive self-improvement.

notes.title: School scolding
notes.body: Two four-character expressions deliver a double scolding: 浑浑噩噩 is muddling through without clarity, and 不学无术 condemns having neither learning nor skills. The polished, admonishing wording makes the speaker sound briefly like an exasperated teacher. One line later, the lecture devolves into the childishly literal threat that not studying will turn you into a pig.

notes.title: From “pig” to a literary pig
notes.original: 西游记猪八戒四大名著
notes.body: Zhu Bajie is the piglike companion in Journey to the West, one of the Four Great Classical Novels. The lyric gets there by association: refuse to study, become a pig, then name a famous literary pig and the canon he belongs to. An insult turns into a miniature reading lesson.

sources.label: Hong Kong Education Bureau: Journey to the West
Education Bureau: the novel among the Four Classics

notes.title: Mind reading
notes.body: Mind-reading would help against another person, but the immediately preceding game is roulette: the wheel has no intentions to read. That mismatch makes the claimed advantage absurd. The verse keeps adding ways to guarantee a win—special powers, hard work, a spell, a brother’s reassurance—without actually changing the chance involved.

notes.title: A familiar song title inside a gamble

phrase.en: You have to fight for it to win

notes.body: 爱拼才会赢 is also the title of the Taiwanese Hokkien hit made famous by Ye Qitian, a phrase widely used to encourage persistence. Here that encouraging motto sits after a spinning roulette wheel and “one more round,” then gives way to a spell. Effort, luck and magical confidence pile into the same attempt to win.

sources.label: National Taiwan University Library: Ye Qitian and 愛拚才會贏

notes.title: An incantation before the next round
notes.body: This formula calls on the efficacy of heaven and earth. It appears between claims of fighting to win and confidence about the next round, mixing supernatural appeal with gambling language.

phrase.en: Spirits of heaven, spirits of earth

notes.title: Sure thing

phrase.en: This round is a sure thing

notes.body: 把 counts a round or game here. 肯定行 is the certainty of “this will work,” and 稳了 just before it says the result is already secure. Repeating that confidence never supplies the winning outcome. It leaves us inside the ritual of talking oneself into one more attempt, suspended between a boast and a plea.

tracks.intro: A lone-wolf boast keeps exposing its own cost: other people become noise, germs and collusion, but being hated still hurts and every consequence must be carried alone.

notes.title: Already understood

phrase.en: Now I know what you're talking about

notes.body: Sentence-final 了 makes this a change of understanding: now he gets it. But the repeated announcement is followed by “don’t give me that bullshit,” so comprehension ends the conversation instead of opening it. The refrain stages someone hearing enough to decide that no further explanation deserves their time.

notes.title: “Fine” turns into “go”

phrase.en: free to go where I please

notes.body: 我看行 means “I think it works.” Beside 神州 in the next line, it also recalls China Mobile’s 神州行—我看行 slogan. The verse reshuffles that ready-made advertising confidence into a boast about roaming freely. 行 xíng keeps changing jobs: approval in 我看行, movement in 任我行. The commercial catchphrase and the ordinary meanings reinforce each other.

sources.label: China Mobile: 神州行 brand and 我看行 slogan

notes.title: Missile / troublemaker
notes.original: 戴上口罩我是洲际导弹
notes.body: 导弹, “missile,” and the following 捣蛋, “make trouble,” are both dǎodàn in Mandarin. The speaker upgrades himself into a long-range weapon, then uses the identical sound to tell younger people to stop acting up. The scale jumps from military threat to scolding a nuisance.

notes.title: Age rank
notes.original: 生日比我小的别在这跟我捣蛋
notes.body: 生日比我小的 makes birth date into rank: being born later supposedly gives someone less standing to challenge him. The line sounds like an older kid or senior colleague pulling age instead of answering an argument. That everyday pecking order gives the lone-wolf boast a small, recognizable social setting.

notes.title: Hip hop test
notes.body: The question sounds like the start of a serious argument over what counts as hip-hop, but the next line insults the listeners as blind. Instead of offering his own definition, the speaker attacks the people who might certify one. The move makes genre authority another social judgment he refuses to accept.

notes.title: Chihuahua
notes.body: A Chihuahua is a very small dog, so the name miniaturizes the target after the speaker has inflated himself to an intercontinental missile. The next line abruptly supplies a husband who never comes home. The insult changes into a scrap of domestic gossip, yanking the inflated boast into another small, unflattering scene.

notes.title: Busy
notes.body: 忙 works first as a defense—there is no time for this—and then as self-advice: better to stay occupied. But “all excuses / all lies” follows soon afterward. The song lets busyness wobble between a useful shield and the very sort of explanation it is sick of hearing from other people.

notes.title: Face versus a line you will not cross
notes.body: 面子 is the public standing one tries to maintain in other people’s eyes; 底线 is the limit one claims not to cross. The lines trade the second for the first: preserving appearance costs an actual principle. Their short, parallel form makes the exchange sound almost like a transaction, a compressed explanation for why this voice distrusts the group.

notes.title: Sharing a nest is an accusation
notes.body: 蛇鼠一窝 puts snakes and rats in one nest: bad actors sheltering together and protecting one another. Its collective picture matters next to the lone wolf. The speaker does not reject only one enemy; he imagines a whole social habitat as corrupt and casts solitary life as the cleaner alternative.

phrase.en: Snakes and rats in the same nest

notes.title: The mask changes jobs
notes.original: 口罩我是一定要戴起的
notes.body: The first mask belongs to the boast about being a missile. When it returns, other people have become a spreading virus, so it functions as a barrier against contact. Read together, the images make isolation both a display of force and a means of self-protection.

notes.title: Why hate
notes.original: 为什么他们全部都恨我

phrase.zh: 为什么他们全部都恨我
phrase.en: Why do they all hate me?

notes.body: The earlier “I only listen to myself” sounds absolute. Asking why everybody hates him immediately reveals how much their judgment still matters. That turn gives the isolation a second register: being alone is both a chosen badge of autonomy and a confusing rejection he cannot explain away.

notes.title: A colloquial exclamation
notes.original: 我勒个乖乖当我看不见
notes.body: 我勒个乖乖 is an emphatic expression of surprise or disbelief. It is not a literal statement about a well-behaved person; “good grief” carries its function here.

notes.title: Carrying the consequences alone
notes.body: 扛 is to carry a load on one’s shoulder; 扛事 extends that bodily strength to taking responsibility. After “if trouble happens,” the promise is to absorb the consequences himself. As the verb repeats, independence becomes work and weight. The lone-wolf pose includes a cost: there is nobody else to help carry it.

tracks.intro: Recipes, classical poetry, utility bills and film sets supply the vocabulary for a furious refusal to socialize. Polite speech and everyday competence make the threats stranger, not softer.

notes.title: An anti-social social club
notes.body: The English title is also the name of the streetwear brand Anti Social Social Club. Its contradiction—a club built around refusing company—fits the hook. The Chinese is 反社交, against socializing, rather than 反社会, against society. It claims the right to reject interaction, then spends the song angrily addressing the people it wants gone.

sources.label: Anti Social Social Club: brand owner’s profile

notes.title: Rough i
notes.body: 老子 is a swaggering, confrontational “I” here, with the underlying posture of “your father speaking.” It lets the first-person pronoun itself dominate the listener before the statement even arrives. The English uses an added swear to carry that force; plain “I’m anti-social” would lose the challenge embedded in who is speaking.

notes.title: Too much
notes.original: 知道的太多整个人都不太好了

phrase.zh: 知道的太多整个人都不太好了
phrase.en: Knowing too much has left me feeling all wrong

notes.body: 整个人都不太好了 is colloquial understatement for feeling completely thrown or overwhelmed: literally the whole person is “not very okay.” That conversational softness sits between the abrasive hook and the maxim about ignorance being happiness. Knowledge does not make this speaker masterful; it makes ordinary participation harder.

notes.title: Paid no service

phrase.en: take the money and do nothing

notes.body: The grievance begins as a very concrete failed exchange: money has changed hands, but the promised action has not happened. That specificity matters before the extravagant punishment fantasy. Distrust here is not merely a fashionable anti-social pose; within the verse it starts with someone failing to do what they were paid to do.

notes.title: Twenty grams
notes.original: 再加少许蚝油和二十克香菜
notes.body: 脑花 means brains as an ingredient, and 凉拌 is to dress and serve a dish cold. Oyster sauce and an exact twenty grams of cilantro turn the threat into a usable-sounding recipe. The calm 少许, “a little,” makes it worse: the speaker handles mutilation with the practical care of somebody getting dinner right.

notes.title: Policing bad words, then uttering a curse
notes.body: 不吉利 means unlucky or ill-omened, language that might invite something bad. The speaker says he must keep someone from talking that way; immediately afterward, his own familiar poem opening becomes a wish for their family’s death. The verse turns its stated concern about bad speech into an example of it.

notes.title: A familiar poem takes a dark turn
notes.body: This is the opening of Du Mu’s “Qingming,” a poem associated with spring rain, travelers’ sorrow and the season of honoring the dead. A listener who recognizes it is primed for familiar verse. Instead, the next line makes the addressee’s entire family dead: cultural recognition becomes the setup for a savage replacement ending.

sources.label: Communication University of China: Du Mu’s Qingming

phrase.en: At Qingming, rain falls thick and fine

notes.title: Polite reset
notes.body: Two routine polite responses briefly reset the conversation after the family-death curse. They are followed almost immediately by another accusation of excessive talking. The etiquette sounds automatic, like clicking through an interaction, while the hostility has never actually gone away. The song repeatedly uses courteous phrasing as a hard cut rather than reconciliation.

notes.title: The mundane bill inside the confrontation
notes.original: 这么做容易耗水费电费
notes.body: After daring someone to act and invoking a society governed by law, the voice starts counting water and electricity charges. The bathos is the point: frightening conduct is measured in household expenses. It also connects back to the recipe-like threat, where mutilation came with cooking methods and exact ingredient quantities.

notes.title: Bad space
notes.body: 风水 concerns the auspicious arrangement of places. Here “the feng shui is off” comes between asking why someone has not left and telling them to go immediately. The supposedly environmental problem is effectively the other person’s presence: removing them is the proposed improvement. It is a spatial excuse for a social rejection.

notes.title: Bitter laugh
notes.body: 苦, bitter, changes what laughter means. After a ghost’s crying and a dog’s biting have reduced the surrounding company to disruptive sounds, the speaker can only laugh without pleasure. The song’s grim comedy allows the same outward noise to register both ridicule and being worn down.

notes.title: Underground, made literal
notes.body: 地下 can mean physically underground or an underground cultural scene. The next lines explicitly reject “culture” and say buried in dirt, making the literal meaning central.

notes.title: Little rest
notes.body: 一下下 doubles the already small interval 一下, giving “just a little rest” a soft, almost coaxing sound. But it follows “buried in the dirt,” and the next line calls the rest a long vacation. The cute diminutive and holiday euphemism make the imagined withdrawal more unsettling than a straightforward declaration would be.

notes.title: Life as a film set
notes.body: Hengdian is a major film-production complex filled with constructed settings for different places and historical periods. The name turns “everything is an illusion” into a place you could walk around: public life looks like scenery and the people look cast in roles. After “I’ll tell the truth,” this is the image that explains the disappointment.

tracks.intro: The performance is also the injury: a sore voice keeps singing about nobody noticing its pain. Small practical needs open into a larger gap between being watched and being understood.

notes.title: Hurt hook
notes.body: This hook makes the tool of the performance its subject. 嗓子 is the throat as the place the singing voice comes from; repeatedly singing that it hurts makes the complaint and the labor happen together. The line’s plainness matters: it asks for no grand interpretation before the verse begins listing unmet needs.

notes.title: Water
notes.original: 我想喝口水没人递给我
notes.body: 口 counts a mouthful: he is asking for a sip, not an elaborate backstage demand. Nobody passing him water condenses the larger complaint into a tiny missing act of care. The contrast with the abuse aimed at the room is sharp: the need underneath the angry language is ordinary and immediately solvable.

notes.title: Forty minutes
notes.original: 唱他妈四十分钟我好折磨
notes.body: A specific duration gives the exhaustion a clock. The performance is work that has to be sustained for forty minutes even while the throat hurts; later, time appears to slow. Instead of presenting the stage as instant recognition or escape, the verse makes the audience wait inside the performer’s bodily endurance.

notes.title: The wrong kind of audience
notes.original: 吸毒的狗逼在台下看我笑话
notes.body: 看某人的笑话 means enjoy that person’s embarrassment or failure. It is different from watching someone tell jokes. After the singer describes standing onstage and needing water, this phrase casts the crowd as spectators to his humiliation rather than people sharing his performance.

notes.title: Online stage
notes.original: 网上的傻逼随意诋毁我
notes.body: The movement from the people below the stage to the people online joins two audiences in the same complaint. In the room, they watch him fail; on the internet, they control the story told about him. The verse keeps returning to a gap between being exposed to scrutiny and being understood or cared for.

notes.title: Understanding as both language and empathy
notes.body: At first, “nobody understands” is literal: the words are Chinese, and the crowd cannot follow them. The shorter 没人懂 later drops the language specification. After pain, no water and a humiliating stage experience, comprehension has widened into care: nobody seems to understand what it is like to be the person producing the voice.

notes.title: A face can “stink” without a smell
notes.original: 我的脸像木乃伊一样臭
notes.body: 臭脸 is a sour or visibly displeased face, although 臭 on its own also means foul-smelling. Pairing that expression with a mummy lets bad temper brush against a decaying body. Alongside the zombie DJ, it turns the live show into a scene of the barely animated: everyone is present, but little human responsiveness reaches the stage.

notes.title: Buddha
notes.body: When nobody in the venue responds, the appeal jumps to the Buddha. 苦苦 intensifies the pleading and carries the sound of suffering; the following polite 请问 introduces the extreme wish for the ordeal to end. The sudden devotional register makes abandonment larger than the room.

notes.title: Blades
notes.body: A simile makes an invisible sore throat feel like a sharp object scraping inside the body. The later blood in the phlegm adds something outwardly visible to that private sensation. Across this passage, each return to “nobody understands” follows a fresh attempt to find language physical enough for somebody else to grasp.

tracks.intro: An infestation becomes a mock public-affairs broadcast, then a snack review, then a grotesque offer of tenderness. Formal concern and filthy bodily comedy keep borrowing one another’s voice.

notes.title: All the rage
notes.original: 听说现在北京流行臭虫
notes.body: 流行 describes both a trend spreading through a population and an ailment being prevalent. Putting bedbugs after it makes an infestation sound like the latest fashion. The joke is already in the first sentence, before the mock civic report begins: a thing nobody wants gets announced with the language of what is currently popular.

notes.title: Hearsay
notes.original: 他们都说是老外带过来的
notes.body: The story arrives twice through hearsay: “I hear,” then “they all say.” The foreigners explanation belongs to this circulating rumor, not to an established account of an infestation. That matters for the voice of the mock reporter: it adopts public concern while relaying gossip, then demands that someone finally explain what went wrong.

notes.title: Beautiful home
notes.body: This upbeat phrase sounds like community improvement or a housing pitch. Yet the nearest residents are bedbugs underneath the boards, so the “beautiful home” momentarily belongs to them. The following talk of building materials prolongs the joke: human domestic comfort and the pest’s successful settlement are the same space viewed from opposite sides.

notes.title: Laughing as an evasion
notes.original: 请你严肃不要跟我打哈哈
notes.body: 打哈哈 is to joke or laugh in order to brush something aside, often instead of giving a serious answer. This is a demand for accountability, not a general instruction to stop being happy. The later blocks of 哈哈哈 answer that demand with exactly the laughter it tries to prohibit.

notes.title: A public-service voice
notes.body: 人民群众 means “the masses” or “the people”; 民生问题 means issues affecting people’s livelihoods. The formal civic vocabulary turns a complaint about bitten bottoms into a mock public-affairs report. That change of register is audible in the language itself.

notes.title: Salty food, idle worry

phrase.en: salted duck eggs, worrying for nothing

notes.body: The line pairs salted food with needless worry, echoing the shape of 咸吃萝卜淡操心, a saying about meddling or worrying over matters that are not your business. Here duck eggs take the radish’s place. 咸, “salty,” and 闲, “idle,” are both xián, adding a second route from the snack to having too much time to worry.

sources.label: Hu Hongxia: the saying in use

notes.title: Heads up, bottoms up
notes.body: 龙抬头, “the dragon raises its head,” names the traditional festival on the second day of the second lunar month. The next line replaces that auspicious upward movement with everyone lifting their backsides: the joke depends on hearing the two images together.

sources.label: Ministry of Culture: the Longtaitou custom

notes.title: Scrubbing away someone’s dirt
notes.body: 洗地 literally means wash the floor; in online argument it also means excuse, defend or whitewash someone’s discreditable actions. Kneeling and using tears make that figurative cleanup into humiliating physical labor. Both the floor and the act of covering for someone remain available in the image.

sources.label: People’s Daily: an example of figurative 洗地

notes.title: Unable to afford another injury
notes.body: 伤不起 uses the same “cannot afford it” construction as 买不起, cannot afford to buy. Hurt becomes a cost the speaker cannot absorb. 牌太大 just before it can suggest an opponent’s status or the weight of the game; after kneeling and cleaning up with tears, the admission makes an unequal encounter sound like a losing wager.

notes.title: To die for

phrase.en: So good they're to die for

notes.body: 不要命 normally means not caring whether one lives—reckless to the point of risking death—but in praise of food it intensifies “delicious.” The English “to die for” happens to preserve that exaggeration. On a track that later becomes literally invasive and violent, the disposable snack-language threat acquires a much nastier neighbor.

notes.title: Read the brand boundary correctly
notes.body: 上好佳 is the Chinese name of Oishi, the snack brand. The phrase divides as 换 / 上好佳的 / 也行: “switching to Oishi’s is fine too.” Reading 换上 as one verb would hide the brand name. The preceding shrimp-stick line makes this a casual snack substitution.

notes.title: Fresh info
notes.body: 新鲜 describes both fresh food and something novel or current. After branded snacks and confidence in the taste buds, information becomes the next thing to consume. The next command switches from tasting to listening closely; the lyric moves between senses while preserving its appetite for whatever arrives newest.

notes.title: Kid ambition
notes.body: 娃 is literally a child, but 你娃 can address a grown person with familiar, teasing or belittling force. Beside “look how happily you’re laughing” and the reported ambition, it makes the speaker sound like someone sizing up an overconfident youngster. The diction shrinks the addressee before the final grotesque threat.

notes.title: A swaggering “I”
notes.original: 老子喉咙里有口陈年老痰
notes.body: 老子 can literally mean “father,” but here it is an aggressive first-person pronoun: an “I” that talks down to the listener. The translation adds a swear word to carry that attitude; it is not introducing the speaker’s father into the scene.

notes.title: Aged phlegm
notes.original: 老子喉咙里有口陈年老痰
notes.body: 陈年 describes something kept for years, often valued when applied to wine or other aged products. Adding 老 makes the phlegm emphatically old and long-accumulated. After so much snack talk, this is a repulsive parody of a carefully preserved ingredient; it also brings the album’s sore-throat and spitting imagery back into the mouth.

notes.title: The last image curdles
notes.body: The final repeated phrase calls the preceding knife-and-phlegm image “postmodern tenderness.” Reading “tenderness” straight would lose the collision: the lyric places a gentle label on a grotesquely invasive act.

tracks.intro: Embarrassment at being bored by a good life turns into artistic self-disgust. Casual hesitation, bodily heat and literary dreams make different scales of disappointment meet.

notes.title: Embarrassment
notes.body: 难为情 is the awkwardness of admitting something in front of somebody else: embarrassment, shyness, not knowing how to say it. Repeated 有点, “a little,” softens the confession before we know what it is. The later admission—that a comfortable life feels boring—explains why the opening keeps hesitating at the threshold of speech.

notes.title: When peace feels uncomfortable
notes.body: 贱 is a harsh self-insult with meanings including “cheap” or “base.” Here the next lines explain the complaint: life is going well, yet the speaker is bored. “A sucker for punishment” conveys that self-reproach more naturally than calling him inexpensive.

notes.title: Ripples
notes.body: 波澜 are waves or billows; an uneventful life is water without a disturbance. 反而 in the next line marks the reversal: precisely because things are calm, the speaker is bored. Later the emotional “climate” becomes restless. The song shifts between wanting relief from turbulence and not knowing how to inhabit stillness.

notes.title: Morning drill
notes.original: 还不如早上起来做早操

phrase.en: get up and do morning exercises

notes.body: 早 appears twice: get up early, do the morning exercises. It offers a repetitive bodily routine in answer to an uneventful life, which makes the solution almost comically modest. Then “hold on” interrupts it and the verse launches into artistic self-sacrifice. The speaker cannot stay with a simple plan for feeling better.

notes.title: Artistic sacrifice, disreputable drifter
notes.original: 你看为艺术献身的盲流子
notes.body: 为艺术献身 is the noble language of dedicating or sacrificing oneself to art. 盲流子 carries a very different social judgment: 盲流 labels people drifting into cities from the countryside, and here its contempt makes the artist sound like an unwanted outsider. Putting the two together punctures the heroic image from inside. Devotion to art and social disreputability name the same person.

notes.title: Getting heated
notes.body: 上火 can mean becoming angry or agitated, alongside its traditional bodily “heat” sense. Here it leads into a restless climate and nerves that will not relax. The word makes the emotional condition feel heated and physical without naming a particular illness.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 上火

notes.title: Cant talk

phrase.en: I don't want to talk anymore

notes.body: He says he wants to stop talking because talking makes him feel worse, yet the song continues. That is the small trap the opening hesitation has become: silence offers no explanation, but each explanation keeps the feeling active. Repeating questions later gives the listener a similar experience of being unable to settle the conversation.

notes.title: Carrying the pot
notes.body: 背锅, literally “carry the pot,” means take the blame, often for someone else. 背不完 makes it inexhaustible: however much blame he takes, there is more left to carry. The same image returns explicitly as 黑锅 in “Snatch.”

phrase.en: An endless load of blame to take

notes.title: A whole life inside a dream
notes.body: The “yellow-millet dream” comes from a tale in which a man experiences an entire life of success while a pot of millet has not even finished cooking. The idiom makes achievement seem brief and unreal. After the burden of endless blame, it compresses a whole imagined career into a moment; the following death euphemism and closing eyes complete that collapse.

sources.label: Ministry of Education: 黃粱一夢

phrase.en: A lifetime of glory, gone like a dream

notes.title: A formal phrase for dying
notes.body: 撒手人寰 is a literary euphemism for death: let go of the human world. Its solemn four-character form follows 黄粱一梦, then collapses into the short, repeated command to close the eyes. The sequence moves from polished literary language to a bare bodily action.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 撒手人寰

notes.title: Changed
notes.body: Chinese can leave the subject unstated; 变了 simply announces that a change has happened. Coming after “becoming what he used to hate,” it can carry changes in the person, the life, or the whole situation without naming only one. The repeated question “what was it for?” treats the change as a cost whose purpose has become unclear.

notes.title: Two kinds of being happy
notes.body: 快乐 and 幸福 overlap, but the first emphasizes feeling happy or joyful; the second can describe a fulfilled, fortunate life. Using two different English questions preserves the widening scale before the everyday “How have you been?”

tracks.intro: A bakery display becomes a tender encounter without deciding whether the beloved is a person or a pastry. Sweetness and sourness remain both flavors and possible endings.

notes.title: Fairytale opening
notes.body: A sunny day, nothing to do, a casual walk: the setup is intentionally ordinary and unhurried. Each short line adds one step until “I saw you” changes the attention. That simple storybook pacing makes the later animated pastry feel less like a sudden explanation than a fantasy growing out of an everyday errand.

notes.title: A pastry that looks back
notes.body: The encounter begins with 像, “like”: the person resembles a pastry. Watermelon-seed eyes and the wheat smell then make that comparison almost literal, until the figure notices him and reaches out of the display. The lyric does not draw a firm border between animated baked good and desired person. Its flirting works by keeping both present.

notes.title: Seed eyes
notes.body: The eyes are made rather than merely compared to something: 做的 turns a human feature into a baker’s small construction. Watermelon seeds bring color, scale and an edible material at once. It is an affectionate miniature image; the body is attractive because the lyric keeps noticing how it might have been assembled.

notes.title: Intoxicated
notes.body: 沉醉 is literally to sink into intoxication, and figuratively to be deeply absorbed or enchanted. The next lines turn that figure into a bodily risk—one breath of the aroma could make him faint. Desire makes even approaching the window difficult, so the confident act of initiating contact has to come from “you.”

notes.title: Icing contact
notes.original: 主动把糖霜沾在我鼻尖上

phrase.en: icing on the tip of my nose

notes.body: The first contact is playful and light: icing on a nose. 主动 says the other figure takes the initiative, answering the speaker’s fear of getting closer. Food stops being something he watches through glass and becomes something shared across the boundary, turning the bakery display into a private interaction.

notes.title: Only two
notes.original: 这间屋子里只有我和你
notes.body: The window-facing public encounter suddenly becomes a room containing only two people. That change in scale helps the reassurance land: the world outside drops away while the heartbeat speeds up. The tenderness is unusually sheltered for a mixtape so often preoccupied with unwanted witnesses, fake friends and hostile audiences.

notes.title: Taste carries the uncertainty
notes.body: Sweet and sour remain literal possible flavors, but the repeated question is addressed to “you,” making taste stand for the experience of getting close. These are also the English titles at the two ends of this mixtape: “Sour” opens it and “Sweet” closes it. The bakery encounter gives that album-wide opposition a playful, bodily setting.

notes.title: Too perfect
notes.body: 太 can intensify praise or say something exceeds a tolerable limit. Here “too perfect” prepares the final reversal: perfection is treated as evidence that a mishap is due. Even this gentle scene cannot end in unqualified trust; suspicion returns as a joke about how stories—and good days—are supposed to go wrong.

notes.title: The expected surprise
notes.original: 不出意外的话该出意外了
notes.body: 不出意外的话 ordinarily introduces a prediction: “barring any surprises.” The second half predicts precisely a surprise or mishap, 出意外. Repeating the same expression with and without 不 creates the joke: an accident has become the expected next step.

phrase.zh: 不出意外的话该出意外了
phrase.en: If nothing goes wrong, it's about time something did

tracks.intro: A shaving cut triggers an imperial emergency; a city’s grandeur becomes pettiness; clothes hide animals or nothing at all. A chain of bodily rhymes eventually pulls the whole strange world back into school.

notes.title: A shaving cut at the imperial court
notes.body: 太医 is an imperial physician. Calling for one after a razor nick turns a tiny bathroom mishap into a palace emergency. 不治身亡 then supplies the formal wording for a death despite treatment, as if the scene needs a news report too. “A bunch of quacks” finally punctures the solemn language with ordinary abuse.

notes.title: Polish eyes
notes.body: 擦亮 means polish or wipe until bright. Applied to the eyes, it means become discerning and do not be fooled. The confident declaration is immediately tested by suspicious friends and a subway with no destination displayed. Across the song, claims of clear sight repeatedly run into situations whose meaning or direction remains obscure.

notes.title: Big city, small mind
notes.body: 大都市 is a metropolis, literally a “big city.” 小心眼 means petty or small-minded, literally a “small mind/heart.” Repeating 国际, “international,” makes the second line sound like another civic accolade while reversing 大, big, into 小, small.

notes.title: No terminus
notes.body: The train is ordinary urban infrastructure, but taking one at random without a displayed terminus removes the part that would make the journey purposeful. After the confident future-facing lines, this small practical absence unsettles the promise. Movement continues without a clear destination, much like the verse’s jumps between street life, secrecy and school memory.

notes.title: Salty choke

phrase.en: A little salty, a little hard to swallow

notes.body: The repeated 有点 makes the dinner complaint sound casual and manageable. 噎 is the uncomfortable catching of food in the throat, so the ordinary bowl of noodles adds another constricted body to this stretch of the mixtape. Its scale is deliberately small beside imperial death and an “international metropolis”: a bad evening includes something as undramatic as dinner.

notes.title: Granddad as an insult
notes.body: The following “I’m your granddad” makes 孙子, “grandson,” an insult aimed at people stealing from the speaker. Claiming the senior generation establishes a taunting hierarchy. Read together, these are not lines about a missing grandchild.

notes.title: Classified
notes.body: A private wish is promoted into classified information. 绝不能, “absolutely must not,” just before it and “no ordinary game” afterward keep raising the stakes. The speaker’s desire is now something that has to be defended from other people knowing it; later, “Topboy” will put ideas into a literal safe.

notes.title: Plotting
notes.body: 处心积虑 describes sustained, deliberate planning with a strongly disapproving force: someone has been working out their scheme. It is heavier than a momentary bad impulse. Paired with 人面兽心, the polished four-character idioms make the distrust sound like a verdict, before the verse jumps back into a coarse complaint about money being tight.

notes.title: An animal behind a human exterior
notes.body: 人面兽心 describes a person whose outwardly human appearance conceals cruelty: a human face and a beast’s heart. The next fox-fur coat changes where the animal is located, putting it on the outside as clothing. That progression makes appearance and what lies underneath central to the passage.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 人面獸心

notes.title: Swearing inside a money squeeze
notes.original: 日子过得有点日妈吃紧
notes.body: 吃紧 means strained or in short supply; when applied to one’s days or livelihood, it suggests a financial or practical squeeze. 日妈 is a coarse regional swear inserted as an intensifier. The line’s pressure comes from the combination of a fairly sober word for scarcity and an angry spoken interruption.

notes.title: The child who sees through the costume
notes.body: In Andersen’s tale, grown-ups pretend that an emperor’s nonexistent clothes are real until a child says what everybody can see. The following instruction here is to keep a childlike heart. Childhood becomes a way of exposing the performance around you, while the fox-fur coat and human-faced beast have already made clothing and appearances untrustworthy.

sources.label: Hans Christian Andersen Centre: The Emperor’s New Clothes

notes.title: Gotham in the mire
notes.body: 哥谭 is Gotham, Batman’s fictional city, whose crime and corruption are central to DC’s setting. 泥潭, a muddy pool, also describes a predicament someone is stuck in. Before the rhyme narrows to one teacher’s spit, the lyric briefly gives the everyday “same old shit” the scale of a whole corrupted city.

notes.title: Four nouns become a rhyme machine
notes.original: 至今忘不了数学老师吐的那一口痰
notes.body: The ending stretches the vowel chain 痰 tán, 胆 dǎn, 烂 làn, 蛋 dàn: phlegm, guts, rotten/bad, egg. Each new image provides the syllable for the next stuttered block. The English preserves the changing words and repetitions, but cannot keep that Mandarin rhyme intact.

notes.title: Guts rhyme
notes.original: 那一口痰能让人吓破胆

phrase.en: scare the life out of you

notes.body: 吓破胆 literally makes fright break the gallbladder; 胆 also supplies Chinese vocabulary for courage. The phrase gives the ending its next detachable rhyme, dǎn after tán, phlegm. A bodily idiom becomes a sound to repeat, just as the teacher’s spit becomes disproportionately powerful in the school memory.

notes.title: Bitter grades
notes.original: 太苦了所以我的成绩烂
notes.body: 苦 can describe a bitter taste or a painful, difficult experience. Placed after the teacher’s phlegm, it keeps disgust in the mouth while becoming an explanation for bad grades. The verse turns school failure into a grotesque sensory anecdote, then lets 烂, “bad/rotten,” become another repeated rhyme word.

tracks.intro: The speaker claims to be above the argument while turning refusal into a taunt. Crying and laughing begin as opposing sides, then meet in one compact Chinese expression.

notes.title: Childish
notes.body: Calling the conflict childish claims the position of someone above it. But the hook keeps repeating the dismissal, and the later “keep crying” sounds like playground taunting. The song’s pleasure is in that mismatch: the voice insists it will not engage while spending the track performing exactly how little respect the others deserve.

notes.title: Everyone has an abacus
notes.body: 算盘 is an abacus, and figuratively someone’s calculations or private agenda. “Calculations” preserves both the arithmetic and the self-interest without adding a literal counting frame to the scene.

notes.title: Mock apology
notes.original: 不好意思我的野心太大
notes.body: 不好意思 can be a genuine apology or a polite preface to inconveniencing someone. Here it introduces the boast that his ambitions are simply too big, so the courtesy sharpens rather than softens the insult. It pretends the opponent’s hurt is an unfortunate side effect of the speaker’s greatness.

notes.title: A chilled heart
notes.body: 寒心 literally makes the heart cold. In this use it means being bitterly disappointed or disheartened by someone’s behavior, rather than physically cold. The preceding mock apology makes the dismissiveness especially sharp.

notes.title: Different worlds

phrase.en: We're not from the same world

notes.body: “Not from one world” denies a shared basis for arguing. It can express incompatible lives or outlooks, but here follows “what has that got to do with me?” and becomes a way to refuse responsibility for the other person’s feelings. Superiority is expressed as distance: their complaints supposedly cannot even reach the same level.

notes.title: The chant turns into an idiom
notes.body: 哭笑不得 means being unable to decide whether to laugh or cry at an absurd or embarrassing situation. First the song separates crying and laughing into opposing camps—“you” cry, “I” laugh—then alternates the single words, and finally locks both into this one four-character expression.

phrase.en: Don't know whether to laugh or cry

tracks.intro: Starting over becomes an order to turn bad, because obedience has not protected the vulnerable. The closing encouragement survives, but the voice offering it needs hope too.

notes.title: Still alive
notes.body: 至少, “at least,” sets a bare minimum after two losses: dignity and the contest are gone, but life remains. It is consolation with almost nothing comforting left in it. The following promise of starting again then takes a bitter direction: survival becomes an argument for becoming worse rather than simply doing better.

notes.title: Starting over
notes.body: 大不了 dismisses the worst plausible consequence: even if things go badly, you can begin again. That is a familiar resilient posture, but the next line rewrites the lesson as “this time, turn bad.” The song borrows the shape of encouragement while replacing its moral destination.

notes.title: One syllable changes the warning
notes.body: 变坏 biàn huài means “become bad”; 变态 biàn tài means abnormal or warped and can also be an insult meaning “pervert.” The line proposes a grim alternative: become bad now or become twisted later. Repeating 变 makes the turn almost sound like a correction.

notes.title: Obedience offers no protection
notes.body: 乖 is the approving word used for someone well-behaved or compliant, especially a child. Applied to an animal that was nevertheless slaughtered, the approval becomes useless. It supplies the passage’s concrete argument for the earlier demand to “turn bad”: being good did not keep this creature safe.

notes.title: The eyes that cannot close
notes.body: 死不瞑目 is to die with eyes that cannot close: an unresolved injustice or regret prevents rest. Here the phrase is pulled apart around the slaughtered sheep’s eyes, and the next line spells out the regret. The image turns the ordinary praise 乖, obedient or good, into something bitter: behaving well secured neither safety in life nor peace afterward.

phrase.en: Its eyes won't close in death

notes.title: Release
notes.body: 解脱 can mean being freed from a burden or suffering, with religious uses for liberation as well as everyday ones. Here the life/death parallel makes death the animal’s only release. That bleak inversion matters to the song’s later recovery commands: the voice has to manufacture hope after explicitly depicting a world where relief arrived too late.

notes.title: Borrowed standing, manufactured credibility
notes.original: 拿着我的头号招摇撞骗
notes.body: 招摇撞骗 means exploiting a show of status or a claimed connection to deceive people. It is more specific than lying: the imposture has an audience and a borrowed source of credibility. In a verse about lost dignity and people asking to be brothers, the accusation makes association with the speaker another thing others might extract value from.

notes.title: Expression, mood and complexion
notes.body: 看脸色 means watch someone’s mood and adjust your behavior accordingly. 脸色 is also the visible look or color of a face. The next line turns that social deference into a corpse joke: a dead person cannot offer a welcoming look, and does not have a healthy complexion either.

notes.title: Brotherhood as a blame test
notes.original: 那请问这个黑锅你愿意背吗
notes.body: 背黑锅 means be made a scapegoat or take blame, literally “carry the black pot.” Here the question puts a price on claiming brotherhood: will the would-be brother actually take the fall? It develops the same carrying-blame image heard in “Self Pity.”

notes.title: Owning
notes.original: 我的固执我的偏执我都认
notes.body: 认 is to acknowledge, admit or own up. The speaker accepts both 固执, obstinacy, and 偏执, an excessive fixation or one-sided insistence, instead of answering the accusation by claiming perfect reasonableness. That is a moment of self-recognition inside the hostility. The next claim that everyone else is an enemy still drives the recognition toward isolation.

notes.title: Cash out
notes.body: 提现 is withdrawing a balance into usable money. It cuts through declarations of loyalty and understanding with a practical demand: make the value real this time. Across this stretch of the album, reputation, favors and brotherhood keep being tested against what actually changes hands. Here the accounting word supplies that test in miniature.

notes.title: Washing a face with tears
notes.body: 以泪洗面 is a set expression for weeping continually: tears become the water that washes the face. The later instructions to get up and discard the baby bottle extend the image into a rebuke against helplessness. The very last “I hope I’m right” then makes the promised recovery less certain than those commands sound.

notes.title: Baby bottle
notes.body: The bottle turns emotional dependence into a child’s feeding object. After ordering the listener to stop crying and pull themselves together, the speaker makes recovery sound like compulsory growing up. It is a harsh kind of encouragement: the tender infant image is introduced only to be discarded.

notes.title: Hope about hope
notes.body: 希望 changes its job across the last two statements. First there is hope in the world; then the speaker hopes that very claim is correct. The final line does not erase the encouragement, but exposes the effort required to offer it. The voice has moved from commanding certainty to admitting its own stake in believing.

tracks.intro: A producer’s name becomes a friend’s martial-arts legend. Modesty, a backpack and an ordinary platform keep the grandiose portrait close enough to everyday life to be funny.

notes.title: Sanmao and 3MAO
notes.original: 我有一个朋友名叫三毛
notes.body: The friend’s name 三毛 is Sānmáo; the official production credit for this track is 3MAO. That puts the name inside an actual creative partnership before the verse inflates it into a martial-arts legend. The credit explains the connection, while the improbable combat portrait works as playful mythmaking around the named figure.

sources.label: Jack Zebra: official Zhuang Zhuang track list

notes.title: No knife: the empty hand
notes.body: 空手道 is karate-dō, literally the “way of the empty hand.” The name gives a compact explanation for the previous boast that Sanmao does not need to carry a knife. The next emphasis on technique rather than strength also keeps the portrait focused on acquired skill.

sources.label: Japan Karate Association: meaning of karate-dō

notes.title: Backpack
notes.original: 回国的时候只背了一个书包
notes.body: 书包 is a school-style bag or backpack, a strikingly modest item for someone arriving with lethal combat skills. 只, “only,” emphasizes how little luggage he needs. Along with the admission that he is not very strong, the image builds an unshowy exterior that the later “god of kung fu” will spectacularly exceed.

notes.title: Low profile

phrase.en: humble and keeps a low profile

notes.body: 谦虚 praises not boasting; 低调 praises keeping a low profile. The narrator, however, does plenty of boasting on the fighter’s behalf. That division is the joke’s engine: Sanmao can remain solemn and modest while a friend supplies the apocalyptic reputation, the anxious spectators and the title of kung-fu god.

notes.title: The audience enters the story
notes.body: “Start recording” turns the listener from a recipient of the tale into a potential spectator with a camera. Later the narrative shifts from “he” to “we” applauding: the scene is as concerned with witnessing the fighter as with the fight itself.

notes.title: Victory faith
notes.body: 信仰 is faith or a sustaining belief, so treating victory as its only object gives competition the seriousness of a creed. It also cuts against the friendly introductory “I have a friend.” The portrait gradually shifts from anecdote to heroic legend through the vocabulary around him, not through a detailed account of any particular move.

notes.title: Platform
notes.body: After war, faith and a martial-arts god, the applause happens on a platform. That plain transport setting brings the action back within everyday public life instead of ending in a temple or arena. The narrator’s “we” also makes the legend collective: a group has been watching and now certifies the victory by applauding.

notes.title: Quiet
notes.body: The closing command cuts off the applause the story has just created. It can address the gathered spectators and the listener at once: after narrating the friend’s power, the voice also directs the room’s response. That small act of crowd control caps a song full of looking, recording, tension and public recognition.

tracks.intro: Sister-in-law and dumplings supply a sound game with a bawdy background. The same voice then becomes a strategist, undercover agent and storyteller proud of leaving no handle for others to grab.

notes.title: A family word in a nonsense loop
notes.body: 嫂子 is an older brother’s wife, or a familiar address to a male friend’s wife. Its sǎozi ending chimes with 饺子 jiǎozi, dumplings; the hook keeps moving between a woman, disappearance and dinner through sound. Later “I don’t want the sister-in-law / just the dumplings” makes a comic denial out of the resemblance.

notes.title: A grand chess game
notes.body: 下一盘大棋 literally means play a big game of chess and figuratively describes an elaborate overall strategy. Here it introduces undercover behavior, a cleaned crime scene and stories told fluently. The domestic dumpling refrain abruptly shares space with the language of a secret operation.

phrase.en: playing a grand game of chess

notes.title: Smooth story

phrase.en: Stories roll smoothly off my tongue

notes.body: 娓娓道来 means tell something fluently and engagingly, while 随口 adds an offhand ease. “Survival skill” makes that appealing ability more ambiguous: he can entertain, but he can also talk his way through a situation. The crime-scene cleanup and undercover identity immediately afterward develop the darker uses of a persuasive story.

notes.title: Leaving someone a handle

phrase.en: anything they can use against me

notes.body: A 把柄 is literally a handle and figuratively evidence of a fault that another person can grasp and use against you. Cleaning the crime scene is therefore also removing other people’s leverage. The same handhold metaphor works without needing to identify a real crime behind the scene.

notes.title: Undercover
notes.body: 卧底 is someone embedded under a concealed identity. The image lets living “in the shadows” sound deliberate and skilled rather than merely excluded. It also complicates the earlier survival skill of telling stories: the public-facing voice might itself be a cover, while the song boasts about how little usable evidence it leaves.

notes.title: “What a talent” after a con
notes.body: 人才 usually praises a talented or capable person; on its own it can also be an ironic “what a piece of work.” Here it follows skill at storytelling, concealment and dismissing things as nonsense. The compact compliment leaves those dubious abilities intact rather than turning into straightforward admiration.

notes.title: Cat mouse
notes.body: The two short declarations assign the roles without negotiation: I am the pursuer, you are what gets pursued. Following the covert strategist, this is almost childishly direct. The song can alternate intricate concealment with a playground model of power, then immediately abandon the chase to argue about dumplings.

notes.title: Bawdy dumplings
notes.body: A circulating dirty joke pairs dumplings as the best thing to eat with a sister-in-law as the best person to “play with.” The near-rhyme gives the woman and the food a bawdy connection beyond this song. Here the speaker insists that he only wants the dumplings, making that familiar innuendo the background to a conspicuously emphatic denial.

sources.label: Wan-Qi Li, Cyberbullying in China (2020), p.338

notes.title: Food becomes biology by sound
notes.body: 食物 shíwù means food; 生物 shēngwù means living organisms, or biology as a school subject. The shared final syllable makes “I like food / I never studied biology” feel connected by rhyme even as its logic swerves.

notes.title: What can you do
notes.body: 咋 is a colloquial “how/what,” and 你能够把我咋样 challenges the listener to produce a consequence. It is the spoken shrug of “what are you going to do to me?” rather than a request for information. The next “play all you want” formula retains that swagger while specifying a boundary around jokes at Kai’s expense.

notes.title: A circulating “Brother Kai” catchphrase
notes.body: 玩归玩，闹归闹 sets up a familiar boundary: fool around, but not at my expense. A 2019 esports fan headline uses the same “don’t joke about Brother Kai” formula for Clearlove. Here 凯 also matches the final character of Jackzebra’s name, 张正凯, already magnified into 凯神 in “Kai.” The stock catchphrase fits his own self-coronation: joking is allowed, disrespect is not.

sources.label: 2019 esports fan article using the catchphrase
Apple Music songwriting credit: 张正凯

tracks.intro: A declaration of superiority develops into advice about attention, friendship and protecting one’s ideas. The voice distinguishes care for real brothers from the performance of calling everybody family.

notes.title: Posture as moral character
notes.body: 行得端、坐得正 declares upright conduct: one has done nothing shameful and can face scrutiny. After “stand high / see far,” its two clipped lines make physical posture and moral confidence share a rhythm. The speaker claims both the best vantage point and the right to judge what he sees.

notes.title: Top boy title
notes.body: Jackzebra named Top Boy among the shows he watches when discussing learning English through the internet in a 2025 Dazed interview. That gives the title a connection to his stated viewing habits. In this song, the opening claim to stand higher than everybody else also makes “top boy” function as a straightforward assertion of rank.

notes.title: Audience spit
notes.original: 观众对着你的脸吐唾沫
notes.body: The audience becomes the instrument of humiliation: it spits at the opponent while the speaker occupies the center of the dance floor. Compare “Throat,” where being watched onstage was itself degrading. Across the two songs, public attention can authorize dominance or expose vulnerability depending on whose body stands in front of it.

notes.title: Question mark
notes.body: A question mark is something he can throw, and 接招 in the next line means receive or counter a move in a fight. Punctuation becomes a projectile. The boast is about making the other person answer on his terms: even confusion can be wielded as an attack rather than admitted as uncertainty.

notes.title: Selling a constructed self
notes.body: 人设 is a constructed persona or public character. 卖人设, literally “sell a persona,” accuses someone of marketing that image to an audience. The following fear of being forgotten makes attention itself part of the insult.

notes.title: Forgotten
notes.body: The accusation against selling a persona becomes a fear of disappearing from attention. That gives the insult a mechanism: pleasing this person and that person is driven by the terror of no one remembering you. The verse presents publicity as a dependency, with the carefully maintained image resting on fragile self-worth.

notes.title: Fragility you can poke through
notes.body: Traditional paper-covered windows supply a concrete image for the previous fragile self-esteem: one poke ruins the surface. The lyric moves directly from an abstract weakness to something that can be punctured.

notes.title: A bird that repeats human speech
notes.body: 八哥 is a myna, a bird known for imitating human speech. 碎嘴 means incessant, petty chatter. Together they reduce the opponent’s voice to tiresome repeated noise; the following charge that culture is “just talk” continues that attack on speech without substance.

sources.label: Taipei Zoo: mynas imitating human voices

notes.title: Shameless, not resilient
notes.body: 皮厚 draws on 脸皮厚, a thick face: being shameless or unembarrassed when one should feel ashamed. English “thick-skinned” can praise resilience, but that is not the force of this insult. The accusation sits beside fragile self-esteem, so outward shamelessness and inward insecurity coexist.

notes.title: Betrayal as a possessing spirit
notes.original: 背刺鬼半夜上身随手做做
notes.body: 背刺 is a stab in the back, and by extension betrayal. Adding 鬼 turns the betraying impulse into a ghost; 上身 says it possesses the body. 随手做做 then treats that dramatic supernatural intrusion as something done casually. The line moves between a familiar social metaphor and a little horror scene.

notes.title: Alone again
notes.body: “Now I see clearly” leads into walking alone, a connection heard repeatedly in this run of tracks: insight costs company. But 走到哪算哪 afterward gives the independence an improvised quality—go as far as one goes, work out the destination later. The refusal to join others does not require a finished plan.

notes.title: A change in the food image
notes.body: 菜 can mean a dish or vegetables, but in competitive slang it also calls someone unskilled. 肉变菜了 keeps the literal kitchen picture—meat turning into a dish—next to the following refusal to keep playing. That juxtaposition allows competence and edibility to blur: the same word can put something on the menu or dismiss someone as an easy opponent.

phrase.en: The meat's turned into a dish

notes.title: Brothers well

phrase.en: things go well for my brothers

notes.body: 顺 describes life moving smoothly rather than meeting obstructions. Happiness at the brothers’ good fortune interrupts the attack on fake people with a plain expression of generosity. That distinction matters when the song later warns against calling everybody a brother: the objection is to indiscriminate affiliation, not to caring about anybody at all.

notes.title: Heaven choice
notes.body: 旨意 is a will or decree with a lofty, authoritative register. Yet the next passage insists on effort, refuses rewards falling from the sky and places the decision in your own hands. The song holds fortune and agency together: some outcomes exceed control, but that does not release anyone from acting.

notes.title: No free pancakes from heaven
notes.body: The proverb says that stuffed pancakes do not fall from the sky: rewards do not simply arrive without effort. Keeping the food image preserves the abrupt shift from heaven’s will to practical advice about working and deciding for yourself.

phrase.en: Stuffed pancakes won't fall from the sky

notes.title: Calling someone brother is a commitment
notes.original: 不要随便跟人称兄道弟
notes.body: 称兄道弟 literally means address each other as elder and younger brothers; it describes proclaimed closeness between people who need not be relatives. After celebrating his own brothers’ good fortune, the speaker warns against granting that status freely. The following “sincerity doesn’t buy sincerity” questions whether the commitment will be returned.

notes.title: Wings
notes.body: Protecting the wings comes before flying: freedom requires preserving the part of oneself that makes departure possible. Then the lyric puts ideas in a safe. These images translate distrust into a practical ethic of guarding capacity and plans, rather than simply winning the current quarrel. The last line calls that an education school did not provide.

tracks.intro: Hierarchy becomes physical: raised dogs, ancestors and forced bows establish a speaker who claims the right to control everything. Kitchen appliances and wordplay make the exaggerated cruelty grimly ordinary.

notes.title: Kowtow

phrase.en: knock your head to the ground

notes.body: 磕头 is the bodily act often called kowtowing: kneeling and bringing the forehead down. Here it is coerced submission, and later the demand continues until blood appears. Compare “Blessed,” where kneeling and joined palms ask for protection. The same lowered body expresses vulnerability there and an imposed hierarchy here, depending on who controls the gesture.

notes.title: The family tree as a threat
notes.body: Claiming to be someone’s 祖宗, ancestor, is a way of asserting contemptuous superiority. 孙子, grandson, pushes the listener down the same hierarchy. The demanded 磕头 is a kneeling bow that brings the forehead to the ground, so the language of seniority becomes a physical demand for submission.

notes.title: Raised dog

phrase.en: A dog I raised with my own hands

notes.body: 亲手 claims personal labor—“with my own hands”—and 养大 means raising something to adulthood. Calling the opponent a dog makes the care retrospectively into ownership: because I made you, you owe me obedience. This turns the mixtape’s recurrent worry about disloyal associates into an especially possessive account of the relationship.

notes.title: A head underfoot, then a ball in play
notes.body: 运球 is the sporting action of moving with or dribbling a ball. Placed directly after stepping on someone’s head and before “life is like a game,” it lets humiliation slide into play. The sequence sustains control over the opponent while making the violence sound routine.

notes.title: Sicko
notes.body: 变态 is a harsh label for someone warped or perverse. Here the speaker claims the insult himself and follows it with liking to get angry every day. That removes the expectation of proportionate behavior before the cooking threat arrives: the persona announces that excess is part of the performance rather than an accusation it will defend against.

notes.title: A real appliance brand inside the threat
notes.body: 方太 is Fotile, a kitchen-appliance company that makes range hoods. After the pressure-cooker threat, the very specific product detail makes the imagined kitchen mundane and recognizable.

notes.title: Friends, tar and anxiety
notes.original: 交友不慎焦油里掺了点焦虑
notes.body: The sound runs from 交友 jiāoyǒu, making friends, to 焦油 jiāoyóu, tar, to 焦虑 jiāolǜ, anxiety. The first two are close in sound but very different in meaning; the shared 焦 keeps the chain moving. A literal English line preserves the bizarre mixture while this note restores the audible connection.

phrase.en: mixed a little anxiety into the tar

notes.title: Crying and “cool” share a sound
notes.original: 哭你妈逼是不是觉得自己很酷
notes.body: 哭 kū, “cry,” and 酷 kù, “cool,” differ only in tone. The taunt turns the opponent’s crying into a question about their pose, closing the line with almost the sound it began with. The English captures the challenge but loses that tight sound reversal.

notes.title: Good fortune catches fire
notes.original: 你家祖坟冒青烟操你妈的燃起来了
notes.body: 祖坟冒青烟, blue smoke rising from ancestral graves, is a saying about extraordinary family good fortune or ancestral blessing. The second half takes the smoke literally and turns the auspicious expression into graves on fire. 燃起来 also works as “get fired up,” intensifying the collision.

sources.label: People’s Daily: the ancestral-blessing expression in use

phrase.en: Blue smoke from your ancestral graves

notes.title: Throat threat
notes.original: 救命救命你喊破喉咙都没有用
notes.body: 喊破喉咙 is to shout until the throat is ruined, a conventional way to say no amount of calling will help. The body echoes “Throat,” where the performer suffered while nobody cared. Here the arrangement reverses: the threatening voice imagines someone else exhausting their voice and declares in advance that it will not respond.

notes.title: Candy
notes.body: Asking for candy infantilizes the opponent immediately after the demand for bloody submission. It suggests someone seeking a small soothing treat in a scene that offers none. The next line also refuses touch, so both comfort and access to the speaker’s body are withheld; the verse keeps all vulnerability on the other side.

notes.title: Safety mood

phrase.en: I take off the safety when I feel like it

notes.body: 保险 here is a gun’s safety catch. 看心情 makes a mechanism designed to prevent accidental firing depend on mood. The boast is therefore about unpredictability as much as firepower: the other person cannot count on a stable rule. That extends the earlier “I like getting angry” into the imagined weapon itself.

notes.title: Morgue calm
notes.original: 挡着我路的畜生太平间里焚
notes.body: 太平间 is the ordinary word for a morgue, but its written parts contain 太平, peace or tranquillity. At the end of a line threatening incineration, that placid name lands with dark irony. The verse repeatedly puts violence inside familiar rooms and household vocabulary, from pressure cooker and range hood to this final place for the dead.

tracks.intro: Painted street lines turn into the artist’s name, while the voice cycles through outlaw, official, tourism promoter, payment recipient and apologetic nuisance. Each new format rearranges who has authority.

notes.title: A street-level warning about fighting
notes.body: The win/lose construction echoes a widely used police warning: lose a fight and go to hospital; win and go to jail. This lyric uses “pay compensation” for the winning outcome. The next “I’m not afraid” answers the warning with bravado.

notes.title: A cheerful V at an enemy
notes.body: 比耶 means make the familiar two-finger V gesture used for photographs, victory or “peace.” It is a hand pose rather than merely saying “yeah.” A bright, camera-ready gesture arrives immediately after the warning about fighting, giving the confrontation a deliberately incongruous expression.

notes.title: Medical check
notes.body: 体检 is a physical examination, but the previous line’s “fallen” life is a moral or social judgment, not something a routine health check could diagnose. The refusal makes reckless living sound like an administrative category that can simply be waved away. It belongs to the opening’s pattern of acknowledging consequences and then declaring them irrelevant.

notes.title: An “eye” for other people’s motives
notes.body: 心眼 can mean shrewdness, suspicion or a calculating intention, as well as the capacity to judge people. 没有心眼 can praise someone’s straightforwardness or expose their naivety. The next lines deliberately provoke and trample others, complicating this claim to live innocently.

notes.title: A moral line becomes a painted line
notes.body: 底线 is a bottom line or limit one will not cross, including a moral boundary. Claiming blindness makes “where is the line?” into an excuse for not observing one. The verse then produces actual white lines on a road: the abstract limit leads into the crosswalk image.

notes.title: How paint makes a zebra
notes.original: 斑马斑马斑马斑马斑马斑马
notes.body: 斑马 means zebra, and 斑马线, “zebra lines,” is the everyday Chinese term for a crosswalk. The sequence paints white stripes on a street, lets them dry, then chants “zebra.” That also brings the artist’s own name into the refrain without having to say “Jack.”

notes.title: Baby home
notes.body: The repeated zebra chant suddenly gives way to a small invitation home. 宝贝 can be a lover’s or a parent’s affectionate address, without the lyric choosing one relationship for us. The softness briefly interrupts a song of fights, trampling and outrageous public declarations, before the wish for a holiday expands into collective release.

notes.title: Everyone
notes.body: The repeated “everyone” and “all” make the instructions sound universal: go play, make noise, empty the gasoline, burn the rubbish, strip and shave. Parallel grammar puts a holiday invitation and reckless acts on the same footing. The passage builds momentum by widening permission until “free and easy” slides into “lawless.”

notes.title: Lawless
notes.body: 无法无天 literally has neither law nor heaven: no human or higher authority restrains the behavior. It follows 自由自在, carefree freedom, so two four-character expressions recast the same release first attractively and then as excess. The song does not insert a clean boundary between liberation and simply doing whatever one wants.

notes.title: Reporting
notes.body: A single 报告 switches the voice from the person issuing outrageous instructions to somebody reporting up a chain of authority. 在此申请, “I hereby apply,” then makes a washing machine sound like a formal requisition. The humor comes partly from how completely the speaker can change bureaucratic roles without changing songs.

notes.title: Money needs washing
notes.body: A washing machine follows the complaint about earning too much money. 洗钱 is the Chinese term for money laundering, literally “wash money”; putting an actual washer beside the money makes that figurative verb into a domestic appliance joke.

notes.title: Needs
notes.original: 保障每个人的生活需求

phrase.zh: 保障每个人的生活需求

notes.body: 保障 and 服务 borrow the reassuring voice of an institution promising to look after everyone. But the pledge soon resolves into a five-A tourist attraction, a destination to be rated and promoted. The grand concern for all people and the language of a development pitch slide into one another, followed by a payment that turns out to be game money.

notes.title: Five A’s is an official tourism grade
notes.original: 目标是打造成著名的5A级景区
notes.body: 5A is the highest grade in China’s national tourist-attraction rating system. The line adopts development-plan language—“the goal is to build”—then follows it with a formal welcome to auspicious land. The precise grade gives the grand promise the sound of tourism promotion.

sources.label: Ministry of Culture and Tourism: 5A is the highest grade

notes.title: Auspicious land
notes.original: 欢迎来到这片风水宝地
notes.body: 宝地 is a treasured or excellent place; 风水 makes its excellence auspicious, favorable to those who occupy it. The formal 您好 and 欢迎 imitate a host welcoming visitors. After the crosswalk’s plain painted street, the speaker has verbally upgraded the location into somewhere that can be sold as special.

notes.title: From official welcome to notification
notes.original: 您有一笔待接收的转账
notes.body: The polite 您 and “a transfer waiting to be accepted” read like a payment notification. 举报 then abruptly turns reception into a complaint: the money is only game currency. The short labels 报告, 提醒, 举报 and 遗言 make the verse keep changing its format, from report to alert to accusation to last words.

phrase.en: a transfer waiting to be accepted

notes.title: Final apology
notes.original: 给大家添麻烦了对不起
notes.body: 给大家添麻烦 is a familiar apology for inconveniencing a group. Putting it after 遗言, “last words,” makes ordinary social courtesy grotesquely inadequate to the scale of the farewell. It also reverses the beginning: the person who feared no consequences ends by worrying about the inconvenience caused to everybody else.

tracks.intro: A security booth, a fan and ornamental walnuts hold a whole passage through aging. Irritation, tenderness toward younger people and a childhood bus ride make the fear of time passing quietly specific.

notes.title: Lemon water
notes.body: The line sounds like a manageable piece of self-care advice wedged between bad luck and the fear of getting old. Its modest scale matters: the speaker can choose what to drink even though the passage soon expands into loneliness, aging and worry. The title’s cheerful beverage holds a much less cheerful routine.

notes.title: Old age and childhood share the verse
notes.body: The lyric moves from not wanting to age into supplements, absent adult children and saving for the future, then looks back to childhood on a school bus. That temporal movement is in the text; it gives the repeated security-booth scene more than one stage of life to resonate against.

notes.title: Complaints
notes.body: 满嘴 literally fills the mouth; 牢骚 are grievances and grumbling. The next “unpleasant smell” gives that verbal bitterness a sensory presence, followed by “no antidote.” The opening makes resentment feel like something one carries in the body, while “bitter smile” returns the whole sequence to the language of taste.

notes.title: Security booth
notes.body: Three plain objects or actions—booth, fan, walnuts—form the refrain. They locate the song in an everyday small room, where little changes except the passing time. As the verses move from not wanting to age to absent children and then childhood, that same stationary routine can hold several ages at once without the lyric explicitly naming its sitter.

notes.title: Walnuts for the hands, not the mouth
notes.body: 盘核桃 means repeatedly turning and rubbing ornamental walnuts in the hand, often a carefully matched pair. The hard shells change color and develop a patina through handling. Here the movement joins a fan in a security booth: a tiny, repeating routine for passing time. The nuts are being worked on rather than eaten, an important distinction in this food-filled record.

sources.label: Beijing Forestry and Parks Bureau: ornamental walnuts

notes.title: Children away
notes.body: 子女 refers to one’s sons and daughters, shifting the implied viewpoint toward a parent’s older age. The next phrase answers the absence with cash for retirement. Emotional distance and practical provision share two very short lines: money can support a life, while the children’s presence is a different kind of need.

notes.title: Younger treasures
notes.body: 后辈 is a relational term: the generation or juniors who come after you. Calling them treasures immediately afterward softens the earlier small-minded grumbling. The song allows irritability and tenderness to occupy the same imagined older voice, then makes saving most of the money part of its future-facing care.

notes.title: The big share and the small share
notes.body: 大头 and 小头 literally mean “big head” and “small head,” but here mean the larger and smaller portions of money. Most is saved for the future; the remainder meets 温饱, the basic needs of food and clothing. Translating them as body parts would obscure this ordinary budgeting vocabulary.

notes.title: Childhood future
notes.body: The future just described involves old age, budgeting and absent children; now the lyric returns to a child who looked toward the future eagerly. That reversal changes what “a fulfilled life” might mean. The adult’s effort to leave no regrets is heard beside the younger self who did not yet know how brief the shared happiness would be.

notes.title: Different stops
notes.body: The bus gives separation an ordinary timetable: people leave together and get off at different stops. The following “everyone home to their mother” is playful, but the “all temporary” that follows makes the same ride into an image of relationships ending. No exceptional catastrophe is needed; different destinations are enough.

notes.title: A bus full of separate destinations
notes.body: 各回各家、各找各妈 is a playful rhyming way to tell a group to disperse: everyone go home, everyone find their own mother. After the school-bus image, its singsong 家 jiā / 妈 mā rhyme sounds childlike, while the different stops give that shared journey an ending.

phrase.en: Everyone goes to their own home

tracks.intro: The bed offers reliable comfort while social contact looks like effort without sincerity. Chosen idleness hardens into suspicion, then into a demand that other people tell the truth.

notes.title: Drifting gives way to confrontation
notes.body: The opening wants an empty mind, a bed and nothing to do. After the clipped list of bad moods, the text turns outward toward unreliable people and ends with repeated threats. That change in addressee—from describing “I” to challenging “you”—drives the song’s movement.

notes.title: A stance of not taking things seriously
notes.body: 吊儿郎当 describes a careless, unserious way of behaving, often with a judgment that someone is shirking responsibility. Here the speaker adopts that description himself and immediately says it feels great. It makes the opening’s inactivity sound like an embraced attitude rather than just a lack of energy.

notes.title: Meditation
notes.body: An empty head and closed eyes can be framed as doing nothing or as deliberate meditation. The isolated word briefly gives the slacking a more elevated name. The next explanation, though, is simply that there is a bed in his room. The sequence keeps collapsing lofty reasons for withdrawal into the immediate appeal of being comfortable.

notes.title: Bed escort
notes.body: 扶 is to support or steady somebody physically. Here the bed becomes a reliable helper delivering the speaker to sleep “right on time.” That gentle assistance contrasts with the social world in the later verse, where warmth is not returned and words cannot be trusted. An object provides the dependable company people fail to offer.

notes.title: Playing dumb
notes.body: 装 means put on an appearance, so this is a performed stupidity rather than an admission of not understanding. The clipped list around it—no energy, bad mood, don’t look at me—makes refusal feel like a status update. Withdrawal is presented through small, self-contained responses that discourage anyone from asking for more.

notes.title: A warm face meets a cold backside
notes.body: 热脸贴冷屁股 describes offering warmth or eagerness and getting cold indifference in return. Its deliberately undignified body image makes the effort look humiliating. The English keeps the image so the rejection remains as coarse as the Chinese.

phrase.en: press a warm face against a cold ass

notes.title: A baffling “move”
notes.body: 操作 means an operation or the way someone handles something. Calling it 谜一般, “like a mystery,” is a sarcastic way to say someone’s behavior makes no sense. “Move” carries that judgment.

notes.title: A hidden motive, pictured inside the body
notes.body: 心怀鬼胎 literally imagines harboring a ghostly fetus in one’s heart. As an idiom it means concealing a bad intention or ulterior motive. “Something to hide” carries the accusation.

notes.title: Social steps

phrase.en: Their social steps are so assured
