notes.body: 稳健 normally praises steady, sound progress. Applied to socializing immediately after “hidden motives,” that positive vocabulary turns suspicious: these people move through relationships too competently to seem innocent. The next storm reveals their faces. The worry is that polished social ease helps conceal what a person will do when circumstances change.

notes.title: Words that do not count as a promise
notes.body: 说话算话 means that what you say counts: you keep your promises. Negating it repeats 话, “words,” around the failure to follow through. The later demand for 真心话, honest words, tightens the complaint from unreliability into a test of sincerity.

notes.title: Honest words
notes.original: 不说真心话的小崽子会被我打
notes.body: 真心话 are words from the true heart, rather than a useful performance. But the demand for them is enforced by a threat to hit the speaker. That ending strains its own desire for sincerity: coerced speech is not automatically trustworthy. The opening wish to be left alone has developed into an attempt to control other people’s words.

tracks.intro: A breakfast pairing becomes a portrait of a slick operator. Favors turn into debts, shared dreams into synchronized calculations, and refusing to participate becomes a form of self-protection.

notes.title: Cant bother
notes.body: 懒得 is unwillingness to spend effort, not necessarily inability. Repeating it for listening and caring makes disengagement sound like an allocation of time: this exchange is not worth the work. That claim gets tested when the speaker admits the others have made enough trouble that he has to push himself again.

notes.title: Act together

phrase.en: put on an act with you

notes.body: 跟你 means “with you,” so the refusal is not only to watch a bad actor. It is to become a participant in the other person’s performance, pretending along with them. The next verse’s “old slickster” supplies the partner who knows this routine too well; withholding cooperation is the speaker’s way of breaking the scene.

notes.title: An old fried-dough stick
notes.body: 老油条 is literally an old youtiao, the fried dough often eaten with soy milk. Figuratively it is a practiced operator: someone who knows the ropes and has become slippery with experience. The title keeps the breakfast pairing audible behind the insult. “Brilliant acting” then specifies the skill this particular old hand has acquired: appearing convincing.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 老油條
Kinmen Daily: youtiao, soy milk and the figurative insult

notes.title: A favor becomes a debt
notes.original: 我可不想欠你一个人情
notes.body: 人情 here is a favor carrying an expectation of reciprocity; 欠 makes it something owed. The objection is not just to receiving help but to being placed under an obligation to this particular person. That makes a seemingly friendly exchange another possible entanglement in a verse about slippery operators.

notes.title: Dog chocolate
notes.original: 你是条狗吃巧克力会死
notes.body: The insult pretends to offer protective advice: because the listener is a dog, a tempting food is dangerous to them. That combines exclusion with mock concern—something desirable exists, but not for you. The following direction to find somewhere cool repeats the maneuver, wrapping “get lost” in language that sounds superficially considerate.

notes.title: “Go somewhere cool” means go away

phrase.en: Go find somewhere cool and stay out of my way

notes.body: 哪凉快哪呆着去 is a dismissive way to tell someone to get lost or stop bothering you. Literally it offers somewhere cool to sit, disguising the rejection as an almost hospitable suggestion. After the dog-and-chocolate insult, the surface concern keeps turning into exclusion.

notes.title: Poached chicken
notes.body: 白切鸡 is chicken gently cooked and then cut for serving; the dish name makes the animal ready for a table. The next line imagines its defiant mouth while alive, then praises the firmness of its meat. The passage changes the target from a person who can argue back into something the speaker can inspect and consume.

notes.title: A hard mouth becomes tough meat
notes.body: 嘴硬 means talking tough, refusing to concede or admit fault. Giving that “hard mouth” to a chicken before describing its firm meat pulls an idiomatic personality trait back into the body. The animal insult becomes kitchen imagery.

notes.title: Focus elsewhere
notes.original: 我的重心早放在了别处
notes.body: 重心 is literally a center of gravity; figuratively it is the main concentration of attention or work. Saying it moved elsewhere long ago dismisses the quarrel as already out of date. The song nevertheless continues giving warnings, so its declared detachment coexists with a desire to make sure somebody else learns what he has learned.

notes.title: A newcomer leaving the thatched cottage
notes.body: 初出茅庐 literally means first leaving a thatched cottage. The idiom comes through Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Zhuge Liang’s entry into service; in everyday speech it describes someone inexperienced and just entering the wider world. Here the next line strips away any expectation of gentler treatment for a beginner.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 初出茅廬

notes.title: No handicap

phrase.en: Nobody's going to go easy on you

notes.body: 让着 someone means give them room, hold back, or let them have the advantage, often out of kindness or because they are younger. Its negation cancels the customary excuse of inexperience. After the literary 初出茅庐, the sentence lands as plainspoken instruction about entering a competitive social world.

notes.title: Their calculations line up
notes.body: 打算盘 can mean work an abacus or make self-interested plans. After the shared sky and dream, everyone’s supposedly common purpose becomes the perfectly synchronized noise of calculating. 神同步 is emphatic internet phrasing for uncanny or perfect synchronization.

phrase.en: The clatter of abacuses is perfectly in sync

tracks.intro: A casual dismissal of a mistake gives way to memory, self-doubt and the fear of losing oneself. The final book image leaves life unfinished and the work of reading it ongoing.

notes.title: Take to heart
notes.body: 上心 is to put one’s attention and concern into something. 没怎么 weakens the admission—“not particularly”—before the next line says things went too far. The understatement makes the opening sound like somebody trying to contain the significance of a mistake, while the rest of the verse describes how hard that containment has become.

notes.title: When “playing” stops being harmless
notes.body: 玩大了 is an idiom for taking an activity or situation too far until its stakes become serious. The literal idea of “playing big” makes the casual promise to be careful next time sound inadequate. That throwaway opening is followed by the memories and self-doubt it cannot simply dismiss.

notes.title: Hoping to get away with it
notes.body: 侥幸 is luck one cannot count on, often the hope of escaping an adverse consequence. After “I took things too far” and the casual promise to be careful next time, it carries more self-reproach than a simple wish for good fortune.

notes.title: From faith to confidence in oneself
notes.body: The passage moves from lacking 信仰, a faith or larger belief, to 怀疑自己, doubting oneself, and finally losing 信心, confidence. The shared language of belief narrows from a worldview to the ability to trust oneself. That progression gives the fear of forgetting who one is a precise place in the verse.

notes.title: Around me
notes.body: 身边 literally locates people beside the speaker, so the perceived danger comes from proximity rather than a distant enemy. The next lines move still closer, into memory and an inner argument. The passage narrows the space in which trust might survive: from surrounding company to the mind, then to confidence in oneself.

notes.title: Inner fight
notes.original: 脑海里的声音不停打架
notes.body: 打架 gives thoughts a bodily action: the voices fight one another. The following loss of confidence makes that internal conflict costly rather than merely noisy. It is vivid language for an argument that will not settle. The ordinary verb makes private indecision feel like an exhausting physical struggle.

notes.title: Forget self
notes.original: 我生怕我会忘了我自己
notes.body: 生怕 is a strong fear that something might happen, and the repeated 我 gives the line an intimate circularity: I fear I may forget myself. After memories that will not go away, forgetting is paradoxically the danger too. The speaker cannot choose which parts of experience stay present, or rely on them to hold a stable identity.

notes.title: Try not care
notes.body: 尽量 means as much as one can manage. That qualifier makes the instruction less absolute than the album’s many “I don’t care” declarations: not caring has become an effort, and perhaps an incomplete one. The promised alternative is endless crying. The sentence frames emotional distance as something attempted under pressure.

notes.title: Life book
notes.body: The image casts the speaker as a reader of life. After mistakes, returning memories and an unfamiliar road, its meaning still has to be worked out as it unfolds. 一直, “continuously,” in the next line matters: he keeps reading. The ending offers persistence without pretending the book has become easy to understand.
